primitives.name: Gaussian conditioning: posterior mean is a covariance-weighted correction and posterior covariance shrinks independently of the observed values (a.14; GP form 2.9-2.10)
primitives.verbatim_quote: Notably, the correction to the covariance matrix does not depend on the observed values.
primitives.page: Appendix A, sec. a.2, p. 300 (eq. a.14); Gaussian process form sec. 2.2, eqs. 2.9-2.10

symbol_and_unit_ledger.mu_1, mu_2: prior mean vectors of the two blocks of a joint Gaussian vector (units of the modeled quantity)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.Sigma_12: cross-covariance between the unknown block and the observed block (squared units of the quantity)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.Sigma_22: covariance of the observed block (squared units); must be invertible
symbol_and_unit_ledger.Sigma_11|2: posterior covariance of the unknown block after conditioning (squared units)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.x_2 - mu_2: surprise: deviation of the observed values from their prior mean (units of the quantity)

assumptions: The unknown and observed quantities are jointly Gaussian, so all conditional distributions are Gaussian in closed form.
The prior mean vector and covariance matrix are known or already estimated when conditioning is applied.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Breaks when the joint distribution is materially non-Gaussian (heavy tails, discrete outcomes), when Sigma_22 is near singular so the inverse amplifies noise, and when the covariance itself was fit to the same data being conditioned on, which double counts evidence.

layer2.mapping: This is the update rule of the whole belief engine: every new observation revises a correlated belief state by a covariance-weighted surprise term, and uncertainty contracts by an amount fixed before the value is seen. In the GSE reasoning engine, player and team strength beliefs are joint states, so one game result must revise correlated beliefs about teammates, opponents, and shared situational factors through exactly this correction, never as isolated point edits.
layer2.telemetry: Game results, play by play outcomes, injury return timelines, and any sensor or tracking feed that reports a value for one component of a correlated belief state.

primitives.name: Automatic relevance determination: per-dimension length scales turn covariance distance into a learned weighted distance, and an irrelevant dimension is nullified by a long length scale (3.24-3.25)
primitives.verbatim_quote: The contribution to the weighted distance (3.24) for that dimension would then be effectively nullified, and the resulting covariance would effectively "ignore" that dimension.
primitives.latex: d_\ell(x, x')^2 = \sum_j \frac{(x_j - x_j')^2}{\ell_j^2}, \qquad K(x, x') = K(d_\ell(x, x'))

symbol_and_unit_ledger.ell_j: length scale for input dimension j (units of dimension j); large ell_j means weak dependence on that dimension
symbol_and_unit_ledger.d_ell: dimensionless weighted distance between two inputs after per-dimension rescaling
symbol_and_unit_ledger.K: stationary covariance function evaluated at the weighted distance (squared units of the objective)

assumptions: The covariance is stationary, so similarity depends on the inputs only through a distance.
Length scales are positive and are inferred from data, typically by marginal likelihood or a model posterior.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Breaks when relevance is not axis aligned (interactions rotate the relevant directions, needing the full Mahalanobis form), when length scales are fit on tiny samples and collapse to zero or infinity, and when a dimension matters only in a subregion, which a single global scale cannot express.

layer2.mapping: ARD is a learned feature relevance gate for the reasoning engine: situational inputs such as rest days, travel, weather, and matchup history enter similarity computations with data-driven weights, and a signal family the data finds irrelevant is automatically damped toward zero weight instead of being deleted by hand. The weights themselves become telemetry, showing which situational dimensions the engine currently believes drive similarity between games.
layer2.telemetry: Fitted length scales per input dimension across rolling training windows, logged with the marginal likelihood of each refit.

primitives.name: Model posterior: belief over models or hyperparameters is prior times marginal likelihood, so data support flows to models through their evidence (4.7)
primitives.verbatim_quote: The model posterior provides support to the models most consistent with our prior beliefs and the observed data.
primitives.latex: p(\theta \mid D) \propto p(\theta)\, p(y \mid x, \theta)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.theta: model index or hyperparameter vector indexing a family of objective models (dimensionless index or physical parameter units)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.p(y | x, theta): marginal likelihood or model evidence: probability density of the observed data under model theta (units of inverse data volume)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.p(theta): prior belief over models before seeing the dataset (probability or density)

assumptions: A model space and a prior over it are specified before conditioning.
The marginal likelihood is computable, which for latent function models means the latent values at observed locations have been integrated out.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Breaks when the true structure lies outside the model space, since posterior mass then concentrates on the least wrong member; also degrades when evidence integrals are approximated crudely, because small evidence errors are amplified by normalization across models.

layer2.mapping: The engine should hold a posterior over its own model variants, weighting each projection model by how well it predicted the data actually observed, rather than crowning one configuration. Game outcomes then shift weight continuously between, for example, pace-driven and matchup-driven model variants, and the shift is auditable through the evidence term each variant earned.
layer2.telemetry: Out-of-sample predictive log scores per model variant per week, stored as evidence contributions to the model posterior.

primitives.name: Bayesian Occam's razor: marginal likelihood automatically penalizes complexity because a model that spreads probability over more possible datasets must dilute support for each one (4.8)
primitives.verbatim_quote: penalty for model complexity, an effect known as Bayesian Occam's razor.
primitives.page: sec. 4.2, p. 71; restated in the sec. 5.5 summary, p. 107 (GP log marginal likelihood eq. 4.8)
primitives.latex: \log p(y \mid x, \theta) = -\frac{1}{2}(y - m)^\top C^{-1}(y - m) - \frac{1}{2}\log |C| - \frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.y - m: residual of observations against the prior mean function (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.C: observation covariance matrix, prior covariance plus noise (squared units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.log |C|: complexity penalty term: log volume of datasets the model spreads mass over (dimensionless, nats)

assumptions: Models are compared through a proper probability distribution over all datasets they could generate, so total probability mass is conserved.
For Gaussian process models with additive Gaussian noise the evidence is available in closed form.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The penalty is only as meaningful as the prior: an arbitrarily diffuse prior can make a good model look complex, and with misspecified noise the evidence may punish the right structure for the wrong reason. It also says nothing about which complex model to prefer when two explain the data equally.

layer2.mapping: This gives the engine a principled complexity budget when absorbing new signal families: a richer situational model must earn its extra dimensions in evidence on real games, and the fit term and the complexity term are reported separately, so a rejected signal is recorded as rejected by evidence rather than deleted. That is the quantitative form of the rule that nothing enters the published reasoning without paying for its complexity.
layer2.telemetry: Marginal likelihood decompositions (fit term versus log determinant term) logged for every candidate signal family evaluation.

primitives.name: Model averaging: predictions marginalize over the model posterior instead of committing to one selected model, yielding mixture predictive distributions (4.11-4.12, 8.64-8.65)
primitives.verbatim_quote: Bayesian model averaging over this space yields marginal posterior and predictive distributions
primitives.latex: p(f \mid D) = \int p(f \mid D, \theta)\, p(\theta \mid D)\, d\theta

symbol_and_unit_ledger.p(f | D, theta): objective posterior under one fixed model or hyperparameter setting (density over functions)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.p(theta | D): model posterior weight earned from the data (density over the model space)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.p(f | D): model-marginal posterior: a mixture over models, generally non-Gaussian even when each component is a Gaussian process

assumptions: The model posterior is available exactly or through samples, Laplace approximation, or a discrete set of candidate models.
Each component model can produce its own posterior and predictive distribution.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Breaks down computationally as the model space grows, since every component must be conditioned and stored; it also inherits the model space limitation, because averaging over a family that excludes the truth only averages wrong answers, and mixture predictive intervals can look calibrated while every component is biased the same way.

layer2.mapping: Published projections should be model-marginal: the engine averages over its plausible hyperparameter and structure settings, weighted by evidence, so a single lucky fit cannot dominate a forecast. The width added by disagreement between high-weight models is itself information, separating uncertainty about the game from uncertainty about which model of the game is right.
layer2.telemetry: Per-model predictive distributions and posterior weights retained for every published projection, plus the mixture variance decomposition.

primitives.name: Optimal sequential policy: value satisfies the Bellman recursion, one-step gain plus expected optimal future value, derived by induction on the remaining horizon (5.15-5.18)
primitives.verbatim_quote: assume the optimality of all future decisions. This is known as bellman's principle of optimality.
primitives.page: sec. 5.2, pp. 99-101 (eqs. 5.15-5.18); summary statement sec. 5.5, p. 107
primitives.latex: \alpha_\tau(x; D) = \alpha_1(x; D) + \mathbb{E}\left[\alpha_{\tau-1}^{*}(D') \,\middle|\, x, D\right], \qquad \alpha_\tau^{*}(D) = \max_{x \in X} \alpha_\tau(x; D)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.alpha_1: expected marginal utility gain from one observation (utility units)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.alpha_tau*: optimal expected total future gain with tau decisions remaining (utility units)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.D': dataset after the proposed observation, a random variable through the unknown observed value

assumptions: Preferences over final datasets are fully captured by a utility function of the data.
Future decisions are assumed optimal, which is what licenses the recursion; the horizon or an equivalent stopping structure is defined.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Exact computation grows exponentially in the horizon, so the recursion is a definition of optimality rather than a practical algorithm beyond tiny horizons. It also inherits any misspecification of the utility: a perfectly optimal policy for the wrong utility is still the wrong policy.

layer2.mapping: This is the formal spine for any multi-step reasoning schedule in the engine: the value of gathering one more piece of evidence is its immediate gain plus the expected value of the improved decisions it enables later in the week. The weekly cycle of usage, health, matchup, and situation layers is a horizon problem, and this recursion is what myopic one-layer-at-a-time scoring is an approximation to.
layer2.telemetry: Decision logs showing, for each evidence-gathering step, the immediate gain estimate and the assumed remaining horizon value.

primitives.name: Simple reward versus global reward: terminal-recommendation utility is the best posterior mean over evaluated points (6.3) or over the whole domain (6.5), and the larger action space is riskier
primitives.verbatim_quote: The larger action space underlying global reward leads to a markedly different and somewhat riskier recommendation.
primitives.latex: u(D) = \max_{x \in X} \mu_D(x)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.mu_D(x): posterior mean of the objective at location x after data D (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.X: full feasible domain of the terminal recommendation (the global reward action space)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.u(D): expected utility of the optimal risk-neutral terminal recommendation (units of the objective)

assumptions: The terminal decision is risk neutral, valuing a recommendation by its posterior mean alone.
A posterior mean function over the domain exists, which for the global reward requires a model that can evaluate unevaluated locations.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The global reward can recommend a point whose high posterior mean rests on almost no data, so its realized value is far less certain than the simple reward's evaluated incumbent; under noise the two diverge sharply, and choosing between them is a real risk posture decision, not a technicality.

layer2.mapping: Every engine output is a terminal recommendation problem: a projection published for an unevaluated matchup is a global-reward act, while restating the best-supported estimate is a simple-reward act. Scoring the engine with the global-reward utility forces honesty about extrapolation risk, because the gap between the two rewards measures how much of a forecast's value comes from places the data has not touched.
layer2.telemetry: For each published projection, the best evaluated-anchor estimate alongside the global posterior-mean maximum, so the extrapolation gap is visible.

primitives.name: Information gain utility: value of a dataset is the reduction in entropy of a target quantity from prior to posterior, equivalently a KL divergence (6.8-6.9)
primitives.verbatim_quote: However, the previous definition as the direct reduction in entropy may be more intuitive.
primitives.latex: u(D) = H[\omega] - H[\omega \mid D] = D_{\mathrm{kl}}\left(p(\omega \mid D) \,\|\, p(\omega)\right)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.omega: target quantity the experimenter wants to learn about, such as the optimum location or value (units depend on the target)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.H: differential entropy of the belief about omega (nats)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.D_kl: Kullback-Leibler divergence between posterior and prior beliefs about omega (nats)

assumptions: A target quantity omega is named in advance; information about anything else earns no utility.
Prior and posterior beliefs about omega are proper distributions whose entropies or divergence can be evaluated or approximated.
primitives.breakdown_regime: A single realized dataset can show negative entropy reduction even though the expected gain is nonnegative, and entropy of a continuous target depends on parameterization choices; the utility also ignores whether the learned information changes any decision, so it can reward learning that has no downstream value.

layer2.mapping: This is the scoring rule for pure learning steps inside the engine: a film study, tracking feed, or situational dataset is worth the expected entropy it removes about a named target, such as which coverage a defense will favor, not the volume of data it adds. Naming the target first prevents the engine from crediting itself for learning things that never touch a projection.
layer2.telemetry: Entropy estimates for named belief targets before and after each major data ingestion, stored as information gain per source.

primitives.name: Multi-armed bandit reduction: sequential choice among uncertain options forces an exploration-exploitation dilemma that any policy must resolve (sec. 7.7)
primitives.verbatim_quote: The agent thus faces an exploration-exploitation dilemma, constantly forced to decide whether to select an arm believed to have high expected reward (exploitation)
primitives.latex: x^{*} \in \arg\max_{x \in X} \mathbb{E}[y \mid x] = \arg\max_{x \in X} f(x), \qquad f^{*} = \max_{x \in X} f(x)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.E[y | x]: expected reward of arm x under its unknown reward distribution (units of the reward)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.f: vector of expected rewards over the finite arm set (units of the reward)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.x*, f*: an optimal arm and its expected reward (index; reward units)

assumptions: Rewards are stationary and conditionally independent given the chosen arm in the classical formulation.
Learning about an arm requires allocating observations to it; there is no free information.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The classical bandit assumes arms teach nothing about each other, which fails when options are correlated, as options in a reasoning engine always are; it also frames value as cumulative reward, which can mislead when the real goal is a single best final recommendation.

layer2.mapping: The engine faces this dilemma every cycle: lean on the best-supported read of a matchup or spend scarce analysis capacity probing an uncertain signal that might change several projections at once. The bandit framing makes the tradeoff explicit and countable, and its regret accounting exposes policies that feel productive while systematically under-exploring the signals that matter late in the week.
layer2.telemetry: Per-signal-family allocation logs: how often each family was consulted, its posterior uncertainty at consultation time, and the resulting change in projections.

primitives.name: Optimism in the face of uncertainty: act on the highest plausible value, the predictive quantile, so uncertainty itself earns an exploration bonus (7.18, 8.25)
primitives.verbatim_quote: the arm with the highest plausible expected reward given the currently available information. Arms with highly uncertain reward will have a correspondingly wide range of plausible values
primitives.page: sec. 7.8, p. 145 (eq. 7.18); Gaussian form sec. 8.4, p. 170 (eq. 8.25)
primitives.latex: \alpha_{\mathrm{ucb}}(x; D, \pi) = q(\pi; x, D) = \mu + \beta\sigma, \qquad \beta = \Phi^{-1}(\pi)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.q(pi; x, D): pi-quantile of the predictive distribution at x (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.mu, sigma: predictive mean and standard deviation at x (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.beta: exploration parameter: number of predictive standard deviations credited to uncertainty (dimensionless)

assumptions: A predictive distribution with computable quantiles is maintained at every candidate location.
The confidence parameter is chosen externally; theory requires it to grow toward 1 over time at a controlled rate.
primitives.breakdown_regime: If predictive uncertainty is miscalibrated, the bonus rewards the wrong places: an overconfident model starves exploration, an underconfident one wastes the budget. The quantile is also a pointwise bound, so maximizing it ignores how observations correlate across locations.

layer2.mapping: The upper confidence bound is a clean operator for ranking uncertain matchup reads inside the engine: each candidate interpretation of a game is scored at mean plus beta times its honest uncertainty, so an under-studied but plausible storyline can outrank a well-worn one exactly when its uncertainty is decision-relevant. Beta becomes a single auditable dial for how aggressive the reasoning is allowed to be.
layer2.telemetry: Predictive mean and standard deviation pairs for candidate reads at decision time, with the beta schedule used and the realized outcomes for calibration.

primitives.name: Thompson sampling: sample the next evaluation from the posterior distribution of the optimum's location, equivalently maximize a random draw from the function posterior (7.19-7.20)
primitives.verbatim_quote: This procedure elegantly addresses the exploration-exploitation dilemma: sampling observations proportional to their probability of optimality automatically encourages exploitation, while the inherent randomness of the policy guarantees constant exploration.
primitives.latex: x \sim p(x^{*} \mid D), \qquad \alpha_{\mathrm{ts}}(x; D) \sim p(f \mid D), \quad x \in \arg\max_{x' \in X} \alpha_{\mathrm{ts}}(x'; D)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.p(x* | D): posterior distribution over the location of the global optimum (density over the domain)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.p(f | D): posterior distribution over the objective function itself (density over functions)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.alpha_ts: one sampled plausible objective function, maximized to produce the next evaluation (units of the objective)

assumptions: The posterior over the objective can be sampled, exactly or approximately, and sampled functions can be optimized.
Probability matching is accepted as the exploration mechanism; no explicit bonus parameter is tuned.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Sampling from a function posterior is computationally hard outside special cases, and approximate samplers bias the induced distribution over optima; the policy is also stochastic, so individual decisions cannot be justified one by one, only in aggregate frequency.

layer2.mapping: Thompson sampling gives the engine a disciplined way to distribute attention across plausible best reads of a week: candidate focal matchups are sampled in proportion to their posterior probability of being the most informative or most valuable, which automatically balances proven lines of analysis against neglected ones without a hand-tuned exploration schedule.
layer2.telemetry: Posterior samples of candidate focal analyses per cycle and the frequency with which each was selected, compared against realized value.

primitives.name: Posterior mean maximization is a degenerate policy: one-step lookahead for cumulative reward reduces to the posterior mean and can lock onto the incumbent forever; two-step lookahead adds a knowledge gradient exploration term (7.22)
primitives.verbatim_quote: In our example, the posterior mean is maximized at the previously best-seen point, so the policy will select this point forevermore.
primitives.latex: \alpha_2(x; D) = \mu_D(x) + \alpha_{\mathrm{kg}}(x; D)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.mu_D(x): posterior mean at x, the pure exploitation score (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.alpha_kg: knowledge gradient: expected gain in the global reward from one more observation (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.alpha_2: two-step lookahead acquisition for cumulative reward (units of the objective)

assumptions: Observations carry zero-mean additive noise, so the posterior mean is the expected observed value.
The failure example assumes the posterior mean is maximized at an already evaluated point, which noisy re-evaluation cannot improve in expectation.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The decomposition is specific to two-step lookahead under cumulative reward; it shows exploration only enters through the second step, and even the two-step policy can still stall from overexploitation, as the book's own example run demonstrates.

layer2.mapping: This is a named failure mode the engine must test itself against: any ranking rule that scores only by current best estimate will re-select the incumbent read forever and call it confidence. The decomposition gives the corrective shape: every selection score in the reasoning engine should be auditable as an exploitation term plus an explicit exploration term, and a score with a zero exploration term is flagged, not trusted.
layer2.telemetry: Selection-score decompositions for engine decisions: exploitation component and exploration component logged separately for audit.

primitives.name: Expected improvement in closed form: the expected gain over the incumbent splits into an exploitation term and an exploration term, and increases monotonically in both predictive mean and predictive standard deviation (8.9)
primitives.verbatim_quote: Increasing a point's expected value naturally makes the point more favorable for exploitation, and increasing its uncertainty makes it more favorable for exploration.
primitives.latex: \alpha_{\mathrm{ei}}(x; D) = (\mu - \phi^{*})\, \Phi\!\left(\frac{\mu - \phi^{*}}{\sigma}\right) + \sigma\, \phi\!\left(\frac{\mu - \phi^{*}}{\sigma}\right)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.mu, sigma: predictive mean and standard deviation of the objective at x under a Gaussian process posterior (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.phi*: incumbent best objective value or current simple reward (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.Phi, phi: standard normal cdf and pdf (dimensionless; density per standard deviation)

assumptions: Observations are exact in this form, so improvement is measured against a known incumbent value.
The predictive distribution at the candidate point is Gaussian with positive variance.
primitives.breakdown_regime: With noisy observations the incumbent is not known exactly and this formula silently answers the wrong question; it also only sees the marginal predictive distribution, so it cannot value an observation for what it teaches about other locations.

layer2.mapping: Expected improvement is the engine's template for valuing one more measurement of anything: a candidate data pull is worth the probability-weighted amount by which it could beat the current best estimate, and the closed form exposes the two levers, raising the expected value or raising the honest uncertainty. Any internal score that cannot be decomposed this way is hiding which lever it pulls.
layer2.telemetry: Candidate measurement evaluations scored with predictive mean, predictive standard deviation, and incumbent value at decision time.

primitives.name: Noisy expected improvement is exactly computable: the updated posterior mean is linear in the observation, so the updated simple reward is the upper envelope of lines in the z-score and its expectation is a finite sum (8.10-8.16)
primitives.verbatim_quote: how can we determine whether a particularly high observed value reflects a true underlying effect or is merely an artifact of noise?
primitives.latex: g(a, b) = \sum_i \left[ a_i \left( \Phi(c_{i+1}) - \Phi(c_i) \right) + b_i \left( \phi(c_i) - \phi(c_{i+1}) \right) \right], \qquad \alpha_{\mathrm{ei}}(x; D) = g(a, b) - \mu^{*}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.a, b: intercepts and slopes of the updated posterior mean at each candidate point as a function of the observation z-score; b_i is the posterior covariance with the proposed point divided by predictive standard deviation s (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.c_i: z-score breakpoints where the identity of the maximizing point changes (dimensionless)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.mu*: current simple reward, the maximum posterior mean before observing (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.g(a, b): expected updated simple reward after the observation (units of the objective)

assumptions: The objective posterior is a Gaussian process and observation noise is additive Gaussian, making the updated posterior mean exactly linear in the observed value.
The candidate set for the updated maximum is finite or discretized so the envelope has finitely many segments.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Cost grows with the candidate set size and the exact form still assumes the Gaussian model is right; the popular plug-in shortcuts the book surveys behave badly in high noise, which is precisely the regime where the exact computation matters most.

layer2.mapping: The envelope construction is a general reasoning pattern: when a belief update is linear in incoming evidence, the value of the updated best conclusion is a piecewise linear envelope over evidence outcomes, and its expectation can be computed exactly instead of sampled. Inside the engine, this is how the value of a noisy signal, a beat report or a tracking metric with known error, should be priced: by how the best conclusion moves across the whole range of what the signal might say.
layer2.telemetry: Posterior covariance of each candidate conclusion with each incoming signal, plus signal noise scales, retained so envelope values can be recomputed.

primitives.name: Probability of improvement: the monotone transform (mu - tau)/sigma shares the maxima of the Gaussian exceedance probability, and the policy is risk averse once the mean clears the target (8.21-8.22)
primitives.verbatim_quote: Probability of improvement favors a relatively safe option returning a certain but modest improvement over a more-risky
primitives.latex: \alpha_{\mathrm{pi}}(x; D, \tau) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{\mu - \tau}{\sigma}\right), \qquad \alpha_{\mathrm{pi}}'(x; D, \tau) = \frac{\mu - \tau}{\sigma}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.tau: improvement target the observation must exceed (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.mu, sigma: predictive mean and standard deviation at x (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.alpha_pi': monotone transform of the improvement probability with the same maximizers but a nonvanishing gradient (dimensionless)

assumptions: The predictive distribution is Gaussian in the exact form stated.
A target tau is supplied; the policy's behavior is entirely relative to that target.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The score counts any exceedance equally, so it prefers a certain small gain over a risky large one, and once the predictive mean exceeds the target it actively penalizes uncertainty, the opposite of exploration; with a badly set target the policy degenerates to pure caution or pure gambling.

layer2.mapping: Probability of improvement is the right internal score when the engine's question is binary, will this read clear a stated bar, and the wrong score when the question is how much value is at stake. Keeping both scores in the toolbox, and recording which one justified a decision, prevents threshold-clearing logic from silently replacing magnitude reasoning in projection work.
layer2.telemetry: Decision records tagged by scoring rule used, with target values and predictive moments preserved for later review.

primitives.name: For Gaussian processes, probability of improvement and upper confidence bound have identical maximizing sets under a data-dependent target transform, so a fixed beta schedule is not a fixed target schedule (8.26)
primitives.verbatim_quote: sequentially maximizing an upper confidence bound with a fixed exploration parameter is not equivalent to maximizing probability of improvement with a fixed improvement target.
primitives.latex: x \in \arg\min_{x' \in X} \frac{\tau(\beta) - \mu}{\sigma}, \qquad \tau(\beta) = \max_{x' \in X} \left( \mu + \beta\sigma \right)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.tau(beta): improvement target induced by exploration parameter beta: the optimal upper confidence bound value (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.beta: exploration parameter, predictive standard deviations credited (dimensionless)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.mu, sigma: predictive mean and standard deviation, implicit functions of the candidate point (units of the objective)

assumptions: The objective model is a Gaussian process, so predictive quantiles are affine in the predictive standard deviation.
The comparison is for exact observations; the equivalence is between the induced point sets, not the acquisition values.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The induced target changes with the data and the model at every iteration, so intuitions carried from one parameterization to the other mislead; the correspondence also fails for non-Gaussian predictive distributions where quantiles are not mean plus a multiple of a scale.

layer2.mapping: This equivalence is a warning label for engine tuning: two dials that look like different philosophies, clear a target versus credit uncertainty, are secretly the same dial under a Gaussian belief, with a conversion factor that drifts as data arrives. The engine should therefore expose one canonical exploration parameter and derive the other view from it, instead of tuning both and double counting the same preference.
layer2.telemetry: Exploration parameter settings and their induced target equivalents logged per decision cycle.

primitives.name: Knowledge gradient: expected gain in the global reward requires an inner global maximization inside the expectation, exactly computable on discrete domains through the same envelope function as noisy expected improvement, and intractable in continuous domains (8.30)
primitives.verbatim_quote: The culprit is the nonconvex global optimization in (8.30), which makes the knowledge gradient intractable except in a few special cases.
primitives.latex: \alpha_{\mathrm{kg}}(x; D) = \int \left[ \max_{x' \in X} \mu_{D'}(x') - \mu^{*} \right] p(y \mid x, D)\, dy, \qquad \mu^{*} = \max_{x \in X} \mu_D(x)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.mu_D'(x'): posterior mean after the proposed observation, a function of the unknown observed value (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.p(y | x, D): predictive density of the observation at x (per unit of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.mu*: current global reward, the best posterior mean before observing (units of the objective)

assumptions: The utility is the global reward, so value is judged by the best recommendation after the observation, anywhere in the domain.
Exact computation needs a discrete domain or special Markov structure; continuous use relies on quadrature over the observation and repeated inner optimization.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Approximation error enters twice, in the observation integral and in each inner maximization, and the cheap continuous-parameters approximation collapses back to expected improvement exactly when the incumbent already leads, hiding the cases where the true knowledge gradient differs most.

layer2.mapping: The knowledge gradient is the correct value measure for evidence whose worth is only realized through a better final recommendation somewhere else in the slate, which is most evidence in a connected reasoning engine. Its intractability is equally instructive: the engine must budget computation for valuing information, using quadrature and cached inner optimizations, rather than pretending a local score captures global value.
layer2.telemetry: Quadrature node counts and inner-optimization tolerances recorded with each knowledge-gradient style valuation the engine performs.

primitives.name: Predictive entropy search: mutual information with the optimum's location is computed in predictive form and approximated as log s minus the average log conditional predictive scale over Thompson samples of the optimum, with expectation propagation supplying the conditional beliefs (8.36-8.41)
primitives.verbatim_quote: The approximation is excellent and induces a nearoptimal decision.
primitives.latex: \alpha_{\mathrm{pes}}(x; D) \approx \log s - \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log s_i^{*}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.s: predictive standard deviation of the observation at x (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.s_i*: approximate predictive standard deviation at x after conditioning on the i-th sampled optimum location being the true optimum (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.n: number of Thompson samples of the optimum location (count)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.log s - average log s*: approximate expected entropy reduction about the optimum location (nats)

assumptions: Optimum locations can be sampled from the posterior, and conditioning on a sampled optimum is approximated by Gaussian expectation propagation through gradient, Hessian, and dominance factors.
The objective model is a Gaussian process with additive Gaussian noise so predictive entropies have the log-scale form used.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Every layer is approximate: the samples carry Monte Carlo error, the expectation propagation fit of the constrained posterior is biased, and the Hessian constraints imposed are stricter than true local optimality, so the score is a well-engineered estimate, not the mutual information itself.

layer2.mapping: Predictive entropy search is the engine's pattern for valuing a measurement by how much it would shrink uncertainty about where the best conclusion lies, computed by simulating plausible worlds, conditioning on each, and averaging the shrinkage. That sample-condition-average loop is reusable far beyond optimization: it is how the engine can price a scouting report by the worlds it would rule out.
layer2.telemetry: Thompson sample counts, expectation propagation convergence status, and per-sample conditional scales stored with each information valuation.

primitives.name: Max-value entropy search: mutual information with the optimum's value is estimated from samples of the optimal value through a truncated normal predictive, with a tractable closed form estimator over value quantiles (8.53-8.60)
primitives.verbatim_quote: This approach overestimates the true mutual information by assuming exact observations, but serves as a reasonable approximation when the signal-to-noise ratio is high.
primitives.latex: \alpha_{\mathrm{mes}}(x; D) \approx \frac{1}{2n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ z_i \frac{\phi(z_i)}{\Phi(z_i)} - \log \Phi(z_i) \right], \qquad z_i = \frac{f_i^{*} - \mu}{\sigma}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.f_i*: i-th sampled optimal objective value, taken at quantiles of its posterior distribution (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.mu, sigma: predictive mean and standard deviation at x (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.z_i: standardized gap between sampled optimum value and predictive mean (dimensionless)

assumptions: Samples of the optimal value can be drawn, for instance at equally spaced quantiles of its fitted distribution.
Conditioning on the optimal value truncates the predictive distribution above, and the truncated normal entropy is bounded or approximated in closed form.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The independent representer approximation behind the sampled values overestimates the maximum by Slepian's lemma, the exact-observation surrogate inflates the information estimate when noise is material, and expectation propagation refinement of the truncated moments adds its own bias.

layer2.mapping: Where predictive entropy search asks where the best conclusion is, max-value entropy search asks how good it could be, which is the natural valuation when the engine tracks projected ceilings, such as a player's realistic best case or a unit's best plausible performance. Sampling plausible ceilings and scoring measurements by the entropy they remove about the ceiling keeps upside reasoning honest and comparable across candidates.
layer2.telemetry: Posterior samples of optimal-value targets per tracked entity, with the signal-to-noise ratio at valuation time.

primitives.name: Gaussian process inference is linear algebra: conditioning reduces to solving systems with the observation covariance, done once through a Cholesky factorization at cubic cost with quadratic solves, and standardized coefficients and the log marginal likelihood follow from the same factor (9.1-9.2)
primitives.verbatim_quote: Gaussian process inference requires solving a system of linear equations whose size grows with the number of observed values (9.2).
primitives.latex: \mu_D(x) = \mu(x) + \kappa(x)^\top C^{-1} (y - m), \qquad \alpha = C^{-1}(y - m), \qquad L = \operatorname{chol} C, \quad C = LL^\top

symbol_and_unit_ledger.C: observation covariance: prior covariance at observed locations plus the noise covariance (squared units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.L: lower triangular Cholesky factor of C (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.alpha: standardized coefficients reused by every posterior mean evaluation (per unit of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.kappa(x): prior covariance vector between the evaluation point and observed locations (squared units of the objective)

assumptions: The observation covariance is symmetric positive definite, numerically as well as in exact arithmetic.
One factorization is amortized across all subsequent mean, variance, and derivative evaluations.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Near-duplicate, highly correlated observations make C nearly singular, producing numerically negative eigenvalues and failed factorizations; cost also becomes the binding constraint as datasets grow, since every new observation enlarges the system for everyone.

layer2.mapping: This sets the engine's compute contract: belief updates are factorizations, and their cost grows cubically in accumulated evidence unless structure is exploited. Any always-on reasoning service must therefore budget refits, reuse factorizations across queries, and treat dataset growth as a compute decision, not just a data decision. The standardized coefficient vector alpha is the reusable asset: compute it once, answer many questions cheaply.
layer2.telemetry: Factorization counts, matrix sizes, and solve times per belief update, plus condition estimates of the observation covariance.

primitives.name: Sparse Gaussian process approximation: conditioning on a modest set of inducing values through a Nystrom low-rank covariance approximation cuts inference from cubic to O(n m^2) and scales to hundreds of thousands of observations (9.5-9.6)
primitives.verbatim_quote: we approximate an intractable posterior Gaussian process with a Gaussian process conditioned on carefully designed, fictitious observations at locations called inducing points
primitives.latex: K(x, x') \approx k(x)^\top \Sigma^{-1} k(x'), \qquad k(x) = \left[ K(x, z_i) \right]_{i=1}^{m}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.z_i: inducing locations, designed fictitious observation points in the input space
symbol_and_unit_ledger.Sigma: prior covariance matrix among the inducing values (squared units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.k(x): covariance vector between an input and the inducing set (squared units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.m: number of inducing points, with m much smaller than the observation count n (count)

assumptions: The covariance is well approximated by its action through the inducing set, which holds when inducing locations cover the regions where predictions are needed.
The inducing values are treated as latent variables and integrated or conditioned on within the same Gaussian machinery.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Regions far from every inducing point revert toward the prior and can be silently wrong; the approximation also flattens fine structure the full process would keep, and poorly placed inducing points waste the entire budget while appearing numerically healthy.

layer2.mapping: Inducing points are the engine's compression discipline: a small set of representative situations carries the belief state, and new evidence is folded in through them. Choosing the representatives is the consequential act, exactly like choosing which past games are allowed to stand for a class of matchups, and the approximation error concentrates precisely where representation is thin.
layer2.telemetry: Inducing set membership and coverage diagnostics per belief state: distance from prediction targets to the nearest inducing representative.

primitives.name: Acquisition functions have vanishing gradients far from data because both posterior moments flatten, which strands gradient-based search and worsens sharply with dimension (sec. 9.2)
primitives.verbatim_quote: This vanishing gradient is especially problematic in high-dimensional spaces, where the acquisition function will be flat on an overwhelming fraction of the domain unless the prior encodes absurdly long-scale correlations, a consequence of the unshakable curse of dimensionality.
primitives.latex: \frac{\partial \mu}{\partial x} \approx 0, \qquad \frac{\partial s}{\partial x} \approx 0 \quad \text{far from observed data}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.mu, s: predictive mean function and predictive standard deviation function (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.partial mu / partial x: gradient of the posterior mean with respect to the candidate location (objective units per input unit)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.partial s / partial x: gradient of the predictive scale (objective units per input unit)

assumptions: The covariance decays with distance, as all standard stationary covariances do, so influence of data fades to zero.
The acquisition function is a function of the posterior moments alone, so flat moments imply a flat score.
primitives.breakdown_regime: This is a failure of the optimizer, not of the score: the global maximum may sit in the flat region's unexplored interior. Remedies are structural, including multistart local search from space-filling starts and acquisition designs with nonvanishing signal, and in very high dimensions the flat fraction dominates everything.

layer2.mapping: Any scoring surface the engine optimizes over a rich space of candidate analyses inherits this trap: scores built only from current beliefs go flat exactly where the engine knows least, so naive search reports that nothing is worth investigating. The corrective is procedural, seeding searches from space-filling starting points and treating a flat score as ignorance, not as evidence of low value.
layer2.telemetry: Score-surface diagnostics: fraction of the candidate space where the acquisition gradient is numerically zero at search time.

primitives.name: Stopping rule: terminate data collection when the best acquisition value net of observation cost turns negative, making termination itself a decision inside the same framework (9.9)
primitives.verbatim_quote: it is natural to terminate optimization when the maximum of our chosen acquisition function drops below some threshold
primitives.latex: \max_{x \in X} \alpha(x; D) - c(x) < 0

symbol_and_unit_ledger.alpha(x; D): expected marginal utility gain of observing at x (utility units)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.c(x): cost of the observation at x, expressed in the same utility (utility units)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.max over X: best available net gain; when negative for every candidate, no observation can pay for itself

assumptions: Observation costs are commensurable with utility, so the subtraction is meaningful.
The acquisition function in use honestly reflects the decision maker's marginal gain, including future value where relevant.
primitives.breakdown_regime: A myopic acquisition makes the rule stop too early, because it prices only the next step's direct gain; costs that are uncertain or lumpy, such as a fixed weekly analysis budget, also break the simple threshold form.

layer2.mapping: The engine needs an explicit stop rule for analysis depth per game: keep digging only while the best remaining line of inquiry has positive expected value net of its cost in time and compute. Without the rule, effort allocation is set by habit and deadline panic; with it, shallow coverage of a low-value matchup and deep coverage of a pivotal one are both defensible, auditable choices.
layer2.telemetry: Per-game analysis effort logs with the stopping acquisition value and cost estimate recorded at termination.

primitives.name: Worst-case regret is unbounded on infinite domains at every finite stage, and convergence on all continuous objectives holds exactly when evaluation points are always dense (sec. 10.2)
primitives.verbatim_quote: Unless the domain is finite, running any policy for any finite number of iterations will leave unobserved "holes" that we can fill in with arbitrarily tall "needles," and thus the worst-case regret will be unbounded at every stage of the algorithm.
primitives.latex: r_\tau = f^{*} - \max \phi_\tau, \qquad R_\tau = \sum_{i=1}^{\tau} \rho_i = \tau f^{*} - \sum_{i=1}^{\tau} \phi_i, \qquad r_\tau \le \frac{R_\tau}{\tau}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.r_tau: simple regret: gap between the true optimum value and the best value actually evaluated (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.R_tau: cumulative regret over tau evaluations (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.rho_i: instantaneous regret of the i-th evaluation (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.f*: global maximum value of the objective (units of the objective)

assumptions: The adversary may choose any continuous objective after seeing the policy's evaluation pattern.
The domain is infinite, so finitely many evaluations always leave gaps of positive size.
primitives.breakdown_regime: This is the pessimistic limit of the theory, not a practical forecast: real objectives have bounded variation, and the result's constructive content is the density condition, which says guaranteed learning requires eventually sampling everywhere, a standard no finite budget can meet on rich domains.

layer2.mapping: The needle construction is the engine's humility theorem: on a rich space of possible game scripts, any finite set of studied scenarios leaves room for an unstudied one that dominates. Guarantees must therefore be stated relative to a smoothness class or a prior, never absolutely, and coverage metrics should report how dense the studied scenario set is rather than implying completeness.
layer2.telemetry: Scenario coverage density per analysis cycle: fill distance of evaluated scenario sets within each matchup family.

primitives.name: The RKHS norm of the posterior mean equals the Mahalanobis norm of the observed data under their Gaussian prior, tying function complexity directly to how surprising the data were (10.10)
primitives.verbatim_quote: That is, the rkhs norm of the posterior mean is the Mahalanobis norm of the observed data y under their Gaussian prior distribution (2.2-2.3).
primitives.latex: \lVert \mu_D \rVert_{H_K}^2 = y^\top \Sigma^{-1} y

symbol_and_unit_ledger.H_K: reproducing kernel Hilbert space of the covariance K: functions whose complexity the norm measures (function space)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.mu_D: posterior mean function after data D (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.Sigma: prior covariance matrix of the observed values (squared units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.y^T Sigma^{-1} y: squared Mahalanobis norm of the data under the prior (dimensionless)

assumptions: The posterior mean lies in the RKHS even though sample paths of the process almost surely do not.
Observed values are noiseless in the identity as stated; noise changes the covariance used.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The identity equates two complexity measures but does not bound either: data that are surprising under the prior certify a complex posterior mean, which is exactly the overfitting direction. It is a diagnostic identity, not a guarantee.

layer2.mapping: This gives the engine a one-number complexity audit for any fitted read: the norm of the posterior mean is computable from the data and the prior alone, and a read whose norm is large relative to historical reads is, provably, a complex story extracted from surprising data. That is the quantitative tripwire for narratives that fit last week's result too eagerly.
layer2.telemetry: RKHS norm of fitted belief states per cycle, tracked against the distribution of norms from prior cycles.

primitives.name: Information capacity gamma_tau bounds how much tau noisy observations can teach about the function, and it grows slowly for smooth covariances and polynomially for rough ones (10.13-10.16)
primitives.verbatim_quote: The correct interpretation of this result is that the smoother sample paths require less information to describe, and thus the maximum amount of information one could learn is limited compared to rougher sample paths.
primitives.latex: I(y; f) = \frac{1}{2} \log \left| I + \sigma_n^{-2} \Sigma \right|, \qquad \gamma_\tau = \sup_{|x| = \tau} I(y; f), \qquad \gamma_\tau = O\!\left(\tau^{\alpha} (\log \tau)^{1-\alpha}\right), \; \alpha = \frac{d}{2\nu + d}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.I(y; f): mutual information between observations and the latent function (nats)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.sigma_n: observation noise standard deviation (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.Sigma: prior covariance of the function at the chosen locations (squared units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.nu: Matern smoothness parameter; sample paths are ceil(nu) minus 1 times differentiable (dimensionless)

assumptions: Observation noise is additive Gaussian with known scale in the stated form.
The supremum is over all designs of size tau, so capacity is a property of the model class and noise, not of one dataset.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Capacity bounds the total learnable information but says nothing about whether a given policy extracts it; the rates also depend on the covariance family being correctly specified, and misspecifying smoothness misstates capacity in both directions.

layer2.mapping: Information capacity is the engine's budget law for data feeds: each feed's noise level and the smoothness of what it measures jointly cap how much any amount of collection can teach. A noisy feed about a rough, fast-changing quantity saturates quickly, and continued collection past saturation is waste that this bound exposes before the compute is spent.
layer2.telemetry: Per-feed noise estimates and effective information gained per collection batch, compared against the capacity curve for the assumed smoothness.

primitives.name: GP-UCB regret bound: universally valid confidence intervals convert directly into per-step regret bounds, giving cumulative regret of order sqrt(tau gamma_tau log |X|) (10.19-10.25)
primitives.verbatim_quote: that if the confidence intervals in (10.20) are universally valid, then we can bound the instantaneous regret of the policy in every iteration by noting that the confidence interval of the chosen point always contains the global optimum
primitives.latex: R_\tau = O^{*}\!\left( \sqrt{\tau \, \gamma_\tau \log |X|} \right), \qquad \phi \in \left[ \mu - \beta_i \sigma, \; \mu + \beta_i \sigma \right]

symbol_and_unit_ledger.beta_i: confidence width multiplier at step i; for finite domains, beta_i^2 = 2 log(i^2 pi^2 |X| / 6 delta) (dimensionless)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.delta: allowed failure probability of the universal validity statement (probability)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.|X|: size of the finite domain in the stated bound (count)

assumptions: Confidence intervals are simultaneously valid at all points and steps with probability at least 1 minus delta.
The objective is a sample from the Gaussian process prior in the Bayesian setting of this bound.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The bound's constants and log factors are pessimistic, the required beta schedule is more conservative than practice, and validity collapses if the prior understates the objective's variability; the continuous-domain extension pays an additional discretization and Lipschitz price.

layer2.mapping: This is the template for honest performance accounting in the engine: if its intervals are calibrated, then the cost of its exploration is provably controlled, and if realized shortfalls breach the bound, the intervals, not luck, are indicted. Publishing the beta schedule and the interval hit rates turns calibration from a claim into the load-bearing assumption of a theorem.
layer2.telemetry: Interval coverage audits per forecast family: empirical hit rate of stated confidence intervals against realized outcomes.

primitives.name: Fill distance controls worst-case posterior uncertainty: the largest gap between domain points and observations shrinks the maximum posterior standard deviation like a power of the gap for Matern-class covariances (10.45-10.47)
primitives.verbatim_quote: the largest distance from a point in the domain to the closest observation
primitives.latex: \delta_x = \max_{x \in X} \min_{x_i \in x} |x - x_i|, \qquad \bar{\sigma}_x \le c \, \delta_x^{\nu}, \qquad \bar{\sigma}_x = O\!\left( \tau^{-\nu/d} \right) \text{ on a grid}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.delta_x: fill distance of the observation set (units of the input space)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.sigma_bar_x: largest posterior standard deviation anywhere in the domain (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.c: constant depending on the domain and covariance (objective units per input unit to the nu)

assumptions: Observations are exact in this section, so posterior uncertainty is purely interpolation error.
The objective lies in the RKHS ball of the covariance, giving the smoothness the rate spends.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Rates degrade brutally with dimension through the tau to the minus nu over d term, and exact observations are an idealization: with noise, uncertainty floors at the noise level no matter how dense the design becomes.

layer2.mapping: Fill distance is the right coverage metric for the engine's situational memory: the worst-supported matchup type is the one farthest from anything studied, and its uncertainty bound is set by that distance, not by the average density of the library. Reporting worst-case coverage per family, and shrinking the largest gaps first, follows directly from this contraction law.
layer2.telemetry: Fill distance per situational family: maximum distance from any live matchup profile to the nearest studied profile.

primitives.name: Learning hyperparameters from data can destroy convergence: maximum likelihood length scales with expected improvement provably fail on simple objectives, and the fix is to inflate the assumed function class or constrain estimates (sec. 10.7)
primitives.verbatim_quote: there are extremely simple (piecewise linear!) functions for which this algorithm does not recover the optimum
assumptions: The counterexamples pair expected improvement with maximum likelihood hyperparameter estimation, the most common practical configuration.
The failure functions are deliberately elementary: a Wiener process sample path setting and piecewise linear objectives.
primitives.breakdown_regime: This is the breakdown itself: adaptivity invalidates the fixed-prior theory, because the estimated model can assign the truth near-zero prior mass in regions never sampled. Safeguards exist, including output scale inflation and priors that keep the model class expanding, but they must be imposed deliberately.

layer2.mapping: The engine's standing warning: a model that tunes itself on the games it has seen can tune itself into blindness about the games it has not. The safeguard transfers directly: keep the assumed variability floored, widen the plausible class as evidence accumulates, and treat any hyperparameter estimate that shrinks uncertainty over time as a defect to be caught in review, not as learning.
layer2.telemetry: Hyperparameter trajectories per model family, with alarms when estimated output scales or length scales drift monotonically downward.

primitives.name: Unknown costs: when evaluation costs are themselves uncertain and possibly correlated with the objective, inference about costs runs alongside inference about the objective and the decision integrates over both (11.1)
primitives.verbatim_quote: The natural solution is to perform inference about observation costs throughout optimization and use the resulting beliefs to guide our decisions
primitives.latex: \mathbb{E}\left[ u(D_1) \mid x, D \right] = \iint u\!\left( D \cup \{x, y, z\} \right) p(y, z \mid x, D)\, dy\, dz, \qquad \alpha_{\mathrm{ec}}(x; D) = \frac{\alpha_1(x; D)}{\mathbb{E}[\kappa \mid x, D]}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.z: observed cost outcome accompanying an evaluation (cost units)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.kappa = c(x): latent cost of evaluating at x (cost units)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.p(y, z | x, D): joint predictive density of the objective observation and the cost observation (per unit of each)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.alpha_ec: expected improvement per unit expected cost heuristic (utility per cost unit)

assumptions: Costs are observable after the fact through their own observation model, so a cost belief state can be maintained.
Objective and cost may be dependent, which the joint predictive distribution is allowed to express.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The per-unit-cost ratio is only a heuristic: it ignores that an expensive observation may unlock disproportionate future value, and with a hard total budget the optimal policy depends on the remaining budget, which the ratio never sees.

layer2.mapping: Analysis costs in the engine are uncertain in exactly this sense: a film pull or a data join may take minutes or fail after an hour, and costly lines of inquiry correlate with valuable ones. Maintaining a cost belief per source type, and ranking inquiries by expected gain per expected cost with the joint model available when correlation matters, replaces fixed effort budgets with learned ones.
layer2.telemetry: Realized cost per inquiry type (time, compute, failure rate) logged against predicted cost at request time.

primitives.name: Constrained optimization: value is expected improvement weighted by the probability of feasibility, observations at infeasible points still carry information, and the recommendation rule (observed, all, or confidence feasible) is an explicit risk choice (11.3-11.6)
primitives.verbatim_quote: an observation of the objective at an infeasible point may yield useful information regarding behavior on the feasible region, and could represent an optimal decision if that information were compelling enough
primitives.latex: \alpha(x; D) = \alpha_{\mathrm{ei}}(x; D, \mu^{*}) \, \Pr(x \in F \mid x, D), \qquad F(\delta) = \left\{ x \in X \,\middle|\, \Pr(x \in F \mid D) \ge 1 - \delta \right\}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.F: feasible region defined by constraint functions g_i(x) at most 0 (subset of the domain)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.Pr(x in F | x, D): posterior probability that the candidate satisfies all constraints (probability)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.mu*: best objective value among confidently feasible evaluated points (units of the objective)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.delta: allowed probability of recommending an infeasible point (probability)

assumptions: Constraint functions are modeled probabilistically alongside the objective, so feasibility is a belief, not a certainty, at unevaluated points.
The factorization into improvement times feasibility probability assumes the objective observation does not itself change feasibility belief at the same point beyond the stated model.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When no feasible point has been observed, the incumbent is undefined and the policy degenerates to pure feasibility search; correlated constraints and objectives break the clean factorization, and a hard feasibility requirement makes the confidence-feasible recommendation rule the only defensible one.

layer2.mapping: Engine recommendations live under hard constraints: data availability, publication rules, and integrity limits define a feasible region that is itself only partially known. The transferable structure is threefold: score candidates by value times probability of being admissible, keep learning from inadmissible-region evidence without publishing from it, and state the recommendation rule's risk level delta explicitly.
layer2.telemetry: Constraint belief states per recommendation class: feasibility probabilities and the delta used for each published output.

primitives.name: Batch optimization: the one-step gain of a simultaneous batch integrates the utility over the joint predictive distribution of all batch outcomes, optimal batches spread around the incumbent, and Monte Carlo gradients through the Cholesky factor scale the computation (11.7-11.16)
primitives.verbatim_quote: In both cases, the optimal batch measures on either side of the previously best-seen point; however, knowledge gradient is more tolerant of batches containing only one observation in this region.
primitives.latex: \beta_1(\mathbf{x}; D) = \mathbb{E}\left[ u(D_1) \mid \mathbf{x}, D \right] - u(D) = \int u(D_1)\, p(y \mid \mathbf{x}, D)\, dy

symbol_and_unit_ledger.x (bold): a batch of b evaluation locations chosen before any of their outcomes are seen (domain points)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.p(y | x, D): joint predictive distribution of the whole batch's outcomes, with correlations between batch members (density)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.beta_1: expected utility gain of the batch as a single decision (utility units)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.u(D_1): utility of the dataset augmented by all batch outcomes at once (utility units)

assumptions: Batch members are selected simultaneously, so no member may condition on another member's outcome.
The joint predictive distribution over the batch is available, which for Gaussian processes means the full predictive covariance, not just marginals.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Exact batch expected improvement is practical only for small batches; Monte Carlo estimators trade exactness for scale and inject gradient noise, and greedy sequential heuristics such as the constant liar bake in a fictitious outcome that biases the rest of the batch.

layer2.mapping: A week of engine work is a batch problem: many analyses are commissioned before any results return, and their joint value depends on their correlations, since two studies of the same storyline are worth little more than one. Scoring commissions jointly, with diversity emerging from the joint predictive covariance rather than from a hand-written variety rule, is exactly this construction.
layer2.telemetry: Commissioned analysis batches logged with pairwise similarity estimates, so realized redundancy can be audited against the joint score.

primitives.name: Multifidelity optimization: cheap surrogate evaluations are modeled jointly with the expensive objective, often with a separable product covariance across input and fidelity, under a cost-adjusted utility (11.18)
primitives.verbatim_quote: If surrogate observations are to be useful, they must provide information about the objective function
primitives.latex: K\!\left( [x, i], [x', i'] \right) = K_X(x, x')\, K_I(i, i'), \qquad u(D) = u'(D) - \sum_i c_i

symbol_and_unit_ledger.i, i': fidelity indices, from pure approximations to the true objective (index)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.K_X: covariance over inputs within a fidelity (squared units)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.K_I: covariance across fidelities; its off-diagonal entries encode how informative a surrogate is about the objective (dimensionless correlation scale)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.c_i: cost of one evaluation at fidelity i (cost units)

assumptions: A joint prior over the objective and all surrogates exists, so cross-fidelity correlation is a modeled quantity.
The separable product form assumes input similarity and fidelity similarity factorize, a real restriction.
primitives.breakdown_regime: A surrogate uncorrelated with the objective is pure cost, and the model only learns that after spending on it; biased surrogates are worse, since high cross-correlation with a systematically shifted surrogate imports the bias into objective beliefs at full confidence.

layer2.mapping: The engine's evidence stack is a fidelity ladder: quick statistical summaries, charting data, tracking data, and full film study are surrogates of rising cost for the same underlying matchup truth. Modeling them jointly, with learned cross-fidelity correlation per source, lets cheap evidence steer expensive effort and lets the engine state, in numbers, how much a summary statistic is worth relative to film.
layer2.telemetry: Cross-fidelity correlation estimates per source pair, refreshed as paired observations accumulate, with cost per fidelity level.

primitives.name: Multiobjective optimization: with conflicting objectives there is no unambiguously optimal point, only a Pareto frontier of nondominated tradeoffs, valued by dominated hypervolume or by scalarizations with known blind spots (sec. 11.7)
primitives.verbatim_quote: It is clearly impossible to identify an unambiguously optimal location, even in this relatively simple example.
primitives.latex: g_{\mathrm{lin}}(x; w) = \sum_i w_i \phi_i, \qquad g_{\mathrm{ac}}(x; w, \rho) = \min_i w_i (\phi_i - r_i) + \rho \, g_{\mathrm{lin}}(x; w)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.phi_i: value of objective i at a location (units of objective i)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.r: reference point for hypervolume and Chebyshev scalarization (units of each objective)

assumptions: Dominance is defined componentwise: a point dominates another when it is no worse in every objective and strictly better in one.
The Pareto frontier is the set of points dominated by no other feasible point.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Linear scalarization provably cannot recover frontier points in nonconcave regions, so a weighted-sum habit silently deletes real tradeoffs; hypervolume methods need a reference point whose choice moves the answer, and every scalarization smuggles in a preference that should be owned explicitly.

layer2.mapping: Engine outputs trade objectives against each other constantly: accuracy against coverage, depth against timeliness, caution against decisiveness. The Pareto discipline forbids collapsing these into one score without declaring the weights, and the scalarization blind-spot theorem warns that the declared weighting scheme itself decides which good compromises are even visible.
layer2.telemetry: For multi-objective publications, the weight vector or reference point used, recorded alongside the output so the tradeoff taken is auditable.
